value.overview: The Brown-capped Vireo (Vireo leucophrys) is a small songbird of the vireo family found from Mexico through Central America and across much of the northern and central Andes to Bolivia. It is associated mainly with humid upland forests, cloud forest, mature second growth, and shaded plantations. In Costa Rica, it is a resident highland species rather than a seasonal migrant. Its softly patterned olive-and-yellow plumage and musical, variable song can make it easy to overlook in dense foliage.
value.classification: The Brown-capped Vireo belongs to the family Vireonidae, which includes vireos and greenlets. Its scientific name is Vireo leucophrys.
value.identification: This vireo is about 11.5 centimeters long, with olive-brown upperparts, a brownish crown, a prominent white eyebrow, dusky markings around the lores and behind the eye, and grayish-white ear coverts. The throat and upper breast are pale grayish white, while the lower underparts are pale yellow. The wings and tail are grayish olive to brownish olive-green, often with yellowish edges. Costa Rican birds may show darker, sootier crowns depending on their regional subspecies.
value.rangeHabitat: The Brown-capped Vireo ranges from Mexico south through Central America and continues through the Andes to Bolivia. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly in the country's mountainous interior and highland ranges, including northern and central areas, with a related form extending south toward western Panama. It inhabits humid montane forest, cloud forest, mature secondary woodland, forest edges, and shaded coffee plantations. Costa Rican records are generally associated with elevations of roughly 1,500 to 3,000 meters.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident. In Costa Rica, Brown-capped Vireos are present throughout the year in suitable highland habitat and are not normally treated as a winter migrant or passage species.
value.breeding: The breeding season is incompletely documented. In Costa Rica, breeding activity appears to occur during at least part of the March-to-July period. The nest is a small cup made from plant fibers, moss, and other soft materials, suspended in a fork of a branch. Details such as normal clutch size, incubation length, and fledging period remain poorly known. Both parents participate in caring for nestlings, based on the limited nest observations available from the species as a whole.
value.dietFeeding: The Brown-capped Vireo feeds primarily on insects and other small arthropods, with berries and other small fruits probably making up a lesser part of its diet. It usually forages alone, in pairs, or in mixed-species feeding flocks. Most prey is taken in the upper and middle levels of forest vegetation, where the bird gleans insects from leaves and twigs. It may hang upside down while searching foliage.
value.behavior: This species is active but often inconspicuous, moving through leafy branches while giving a short, pleasant, and somewhat variable warbling song. It commonly joins mixed-species flocks in upland forest and may forage in isolated trees or along forest edges. Its behavior includes careful gleaning and probing of vegetation, sometimes from unusual hanging positions. Because it spends much time within dense foliage, vocal detection is often easier than obtaining a clear view.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is thought to be decreasing, although the species remains widespread and is not currently considered at immediate risk of extinction.
